title: Question 8
stem: Explain the main principles behind the use of nuclear magnetic resonance imaging (NMRI) to obtain diagnostic information about internal body structures.

markscheme_points.text: R.F. or pulse is at Larmor frequency/frequency of precession
allows position of nuclei to be located
allows for location of detection to be changed/different slices to be studied
any two of the points marked (1)

hints: Hint 1: Start by thinking about which nuclei in the body are used for NMRI and why hydrogen in water and tissue is so useful.
Hint 2: Recall what happens to the magnetic moments of those nuclei when the patient is placed in a very strong uniform magnetic field.
Hint 3: Think about the type of electromagnetic pulse that must be applied to interact with the precessing nuclei.
Hint 4: Remember the special frequency condition that must be met for the nuclei to absorb energy strongly - link it to the precession frequency.
Hint 5: Consider what the excited nuclei do once the external pulse is switched off and what they give out.
Hint 6: Think about how the detected signal is used and why different tissues give different diagnostic information.
Hint 7: Ask yourself why a perfectly uniform field alone cannot form an image and what type of additional field is needed.
Hint 8: Link the variation of field strength with position to locating signals and imaging different slices through the body.
parts.proper_answer: A strong uniform magnetic field causes hydrogen nuclei to precess about the field direction at the Larmor frequency. A radio-frequency pulse at the Larmor frequency causes resonance and excitation as nuclei absorb energy. On relaxation the nuclei emit RF radiation which is detected and processed to form an image. A superimposed non-uniform gradient field allows the position of the nuclei to be located and different slices to be studied.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Setting Up Precession in a Strong Field**
You are looking at hydrogen nuclei, mainly protons in water and tissue, because the body contains a lot of water. Each proton behaves like a tiny magnet with spin. When placed in a strong uniform magnetic field, typically from a superconducting magnet, the nuclei align and precess about the field direction, just like a spinning top wobbles about vertical. The precession frequency is the Larmor frequency, given by $$f = \frac{\gamma B}{2\pi}$$ where $B$ is the magnetic flux density.

Step 2: **Driving Resonance with an RF Pulse**
Next a pulse of radio-frequency radiation is applied. For strong absorption, or resonance, the RF must be at exactly the Larmor frequency, equal to the precession frequency. This is the meaning of nuclear magnetic resonance. The nuclei absorb energy from the RF pulse and are excited to a higher energy state, tipping their magnetisation away from the main field direction.

Step 3: **Relaxation and Detection of the Emitted Signal**
When the RF pulse is switched off, the excited nuclei relax back to the lower energy state. During de-excitation they emit RF radiation at the Larmor frequency. Coils around the patient detect this emitted RF pulse. The signal is amplified and processed by computer. Different tissues contain different densities of hydrogen and have different relaxation times, so the strength and timing of the emission varies and gives contrast for diagnostic information.

Step 4: **Locating the Signal with a Gradient Field**
A uniform field alone would make all nuclei precess at the same frequency, so you could not tell where the signal came from. A non-uniform gradient field is superimposed on the strong uniform field. This makes $B$, and therefore the Larmor frequency, vary with position. Only nuclei in a region where the RF matches the local Larmor frequency resonate, so the position of the nuclei can be located.

Step 5: **Building an Image of Slices**
By changing the gradient, the region of resonance can be moved to select different slices through the body. Scanning the detection in this way builds up a 3D map of hydrogen distribution and relaxation behaviour, which is displayed as a detailed image of internal soft-tissue structures without using ionising radiation.

gradient non-uniform field for spatial localisation and slicing
